To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
RecA is stabilized at pH 6.5-8.5 in all buffers tested, and this is not due to secondary structural changes.
RecA in 50 mM HEPES, phosphate, Tris and MES is stabilized up to 50oC above the Tris Tm.

RecA is stabilized by high concentrations of salts, and that this stabilization is due to the Hofmeister series, and that the stabilization is due to a decrease in positive charge on the protein surface.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of buffers on protein stability.
the stability and function of RecA in various buffers.
the effects of buffers, pH and temperature on the thermal stability of RecA and the ability of RecA to bind cofactors and nucleate on DNA.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pH and buffers stabilize RecA by decreasing the positive charge and/or by buffer interactions.
the Hofmeister effect on RecA is not due to a specific anion, but rather to an increase in ionic strength.
RecA is more stable in HEPES, and less stable in phosphate buffer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Hofmeister series of salts and buffers stabilize RecA in the same way, by decreasing the positive charge of RecA.
the Hofmeister effects of high concentrations of salts are due to the charge on the anions and that the pH and buffer effects are due to the pH and buffer properties.
the Hofmeister effect on protein stability and function is a result of both the Hofmeister ion series and the pH of the buffer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the stability of RecA can be increased by using buffers that decrease the positive charge.
the Hofmeister series is not the sole factor in protein stabilization.
RecA is more stable and has a decreased ability to nucleation in the presence of buffers, but this does not correlate with changes in the secondary or tertiary structure of RecA.
